Question: If \(b\gt1,\) \(x\gt0,\) and \((2x)^{\log_b2}-(3x)^{\log_b3}=0,\) then \(x\) is
Solution:
Since \(x>0\), both terms are positive. Taking a logarithm turns their exponents into factors, which makes the equation linear in \(\log_b x\).

Let
\[
u=\log_b2,\qquad v=\log_b3,\qquad t=\log_bx.
\]
The original equation says \((2x)^u=(3x)^v\). Taking \(\log_b\) of both sides and using the product and power rules gives
\[
u(u+t)=v(v+t).
\]
Move everything to one side and factor the difference of squares:
\[
\begin{aligned}
u^2-v^2+t(u-v)&=0,\\
(u-v)(u+v+t)&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
We have \(u\ne v\), since equal logarithms would imply \(2=3\). Thus
\[
t=-(u+v)=-\log_b6=\log_b\frac16.
\]
Consequently \(x=1/6\). All steps are reversible for \(b>1\) and \(x>0\), so this value is the unique solution. The answer is choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
